featured.title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
featured.abstract: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.

insight.tldr: The paper introduces Pro-Memory, a cognitively inspired memory framework that equips proactive LLM agents with prospective memory to retain future intentions and realize them at the right time.
insight.problem: Most existing LLM agent memory systems are retrospective—they retrieve past information to inform current decisions—which fails to address the needs of proactive agents that must remember future-directed intentions and decide when to act without explicit user requests.
insight.approach: The authors propose Pro-Memory, a framework that separates the maintenance of future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. It preserves pending objectives with supporting evidence, assesses new observations against activation conditions, updates intention states based on actions or resolution, and uses an experience memory to distill feedback from completed episodes.
key_findings: Experiments across two benchmarks (delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance) show consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches.
The framework operates successfully across multiple LLM backbones.
It limits unnecessary interventions while timing actions appropriately.
insight.limitations: The current study focuses primarily on text-based proactive interactions rather than multimodal signals (like images, audio, and video), and does not yet address complex long-horizon scenarios with interdependent intentions or real-world safety guarantees.
insight.why_it_matters: For LLM agents and conversational dialogue systems, transitioning from passive retrospective retrieval to active prospective memory is crucial for enabling proactive assistance, allowing agents to initiate helpful actions at the correct moment without causing disruptive or premature interventions.

featured.title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
featured.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: https://rethinking-agentic-rl.github.io/

insight.tldr: Multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning improves long-horizon LLM agent performance, but these gains heavily depend on having sufficient interaction turn budgets.
insight.problem: It is poorly understood what capabilities multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) actually improves in LLM agents, and how reliable these agents are under realistic interaction constraints.
insight.approach: The authors evaluate agentic RL using Pass@(K,T) metrics across sampling breadth (K) and interaction depth (T), analyze step-level action quality, and introduce BudgetMix RL to vary interaction budgets during training.
key_findings: Trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets and diminish significantly when budgets tighten.
Agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience.
BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings by varying interaction budgets during training.
insight.limitations: The gains of agentic RL shrink under tight interaction budgets, and single-step action quality does not consistently improve, presenting deployment risks in applications with strict budgets or irreversible actions.
insight.why_it_matters: It demonstrates that LLM agents and conversational systems evaluated solely on final task success may fail under tight interaction constraints, highlighting the need to evaluate robustness across execution constraints and individual decision reliability.

featured.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
featured.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.

insight.tldr: The paper introduces WASP-Mem, a training-free method that consolidates execution traces and feedback into persistent wiki pages to improve LLM agent procedural memory.
insight.problem: Large language model (LLM) agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static harnesses cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that only appear during execution.
insight.approach: The authors propose WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), which distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages to enable continual agent learning without changing model parameters.
key_findings: WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage.
Prescriptive knowledge organization, such as human-defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules, hurts performance.
Human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement.
A single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%.
insight.limitations: Not stated in the provided text.
insight.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an effective, training-free method for long-term procedural memory management in LLM agents, outlining a clear division of labor where agents organize memory and humans focus selectively on failure diagnosis.

more.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
more.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

more.title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
more.abstract: Large language models increasingly automate complex tasks, but human decision capacity does not scale with their capabilities. In many applications, humans remain essential for providing private context, authority, or judgments unavailable to the agent. We formulate human decision capacity allocation: given multiple consultation opportunities and a limited budget, at which decisions should an LLM agent consult a human? The central challenge is estimating consultation value, which is executor-dependent because the same human input may benefit different downstream agents differently. We introduce Consultation Value Distillation (CVD), which estimates consultation values offline using Monte Carlo executor rollouts and distills these values into lightweight predictors for budgeted allocation, requiring no rollout-based value estimation at deployment. Across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors, CVD improves allocation through joint and continuation-aware value learning, while independent consultation values remain competitive in several settings. CVD also broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, remains robust with substantially less rollout supervision, and enables nearly lossless approximate allocation at low search cost.

more.title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis
more.abstract: Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.

more.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
more.abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

more.title: Do Multi-Turn Conversational Capabilities Carry Over from Text to Speech? A Parallel Multilingual Benchmark
more.abstract: Successful multi-turn voice interaction requires models to retain information from earlier turns, follow persistent instructions, and track revisions to conversational state. These abilities are usually evaluated from transcripts, leaving open whether successes demonstrated from text carry over when the same turns are spoken, and whether this transfer is consistent across languages. We introduce Omnilingua-AudioMC, a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge, to study this question. The benchmark contains 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items across ten languages, with content, turn structure, cross-turn dependencies, and evaluation criteria aligned across transcript and speech conditions. Across six speech-language models, the shift from reference transcripts to direct speech input is strongly model- and language-dependent: models with similar transcript performance can diverge substantially under speech, and their relative strengths across languages can change. Paired rubric-level analysis shows that aggregate transcript-speech gaps can obscure which conversational requirements are preserved, because losses of transcript-demonstrated successes can be offset by gains on other items. Replacing preceding user turns, the current turn, or both with model-generated transcripts localizes recoverable degradation: for the two models with the largest gaps, history substitution yields a larger macro-level improvement than current-turn substitution in all ten languages, while the strongest direct-speech model gains little from either. These results show that transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability and identify the representation of preceding spoken context as an important source of recoverable degradation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-AudioMC.

more.title: Same Rule, Different Verdicts: Rubric Language and Clause Structure in LLM Judges for Korean Support Dialogues
more.abstract: Services that operate in Korean often write their evaluation rubrics in Korean and hand them to an LLM judge. We test whether a judge's verdict depends on the language of the rubric and on how a rubric item is phrased. We write 12 criteria for support dialogues in four clause structures (affirmative, negated, conditional, exception) such that two pairs of structures have the same meaning, and we give each item in Korean and in English. Six low-cost models from three providers, plus one reference model, judge 60 translated ESConv dialogues and 144 constructed boundary cases under every combination (51,744 requests across the seven models). The analysis plan was fixed and committed before data collection. Cross-provider agreement is lower with Korean rubrics than with English rubrics (Cohen's kappa 0.687 vs. 0.745; difference -0.058, 95% CI [-0.072,-0.045]). Disagreement concentrates in negated, conditional, and exception items (odds ratio 5.6 relative to affirmative items). A single model changes its verdict between two items with the same meaning in 11-15% of cases. Two hypotheses are not supported: models from the same provider do not agree more than models from different providers, and adding paired examples does not reduce the language gap. We measure consistency only; no human labels are used, and all materials were drafted by an LLM.

featured.title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
featured.abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models alternates between generating responses and training the policy. These stages place different demands on GPUs, creating opportunities to reduce clock frequency with little loss in throughput. Selecting frequencies online is difficult because response lengths change and frequency trials themselves consume time and energy. We present EE-RL (energy-efficient RL), an online controller that selects separate frequencies for generation and training during RL execution. It compares candidate settings with a prediction of the default GPU governor on the same token workload, and keeps the most energy-efficient setting that meets a throughput threshold. The controller then monitors throughput and energy and adjusts frequencies as the workload changes. Fixed-frequency sweeps on H100 and GB200 show GPU energy savings of up to 28.2% per valid training token across synchronous and asynchronous execution, while largely preserving throughput. EE-RL turns this headroom into online savings, reducing GPU energy per valid training token by up to 16.9% at a modest throughput cost.

insight.tldr: EE-RL is an online controller that dynamically selects separate GPU clock frequencies for the generation and training phases of large language model reinforcement learning, reducing energy consumption while preserving throughput.
insight.problem: Reinforcement learning for large language models alternates between generation and training phases that have different hardware demands. The default GPU governor runs everything near peak clock frequency, causing memory-bound and waiting phases to consume excessive power without proportional throughput gains, while manual frequency tuning is too expensive and complex.
insight.approach: The authors introduce EE-RL (energy-efficient RL), an online controller that measures energy per valid training token (response tokens consumed by training that contribute to the loss) and throughput. It tests candidate frequency settings against the default GPU governor in short trials, selects the most energy-efficient setting within a throughput limit, and continuously adjusts frequencies as the workload changes.
key_findings: Fixed-frequency sweeps on H100 and GB200 show GPU energy savings of up to 28.2% per valid training token across synchronous and asynchronous execution while largely preserving throughput.
EE-RL turns this hardware headroom into online savings, reducing GPU energy per valid training token by up to 16.9% at a modest throughput cost.
Different RL phases (autoregressive generation vs. parallel training batch processing) expose distinct arithmetic intensities and hardware demands.
Post-training an Olmo 3 32B model used 17x more datacenter energy than its instruction-tuned counterpart, highlighting the need for phase-aware energy optimization.
insight.limitations: Not stated in the provided text.
insight.why_it_matters: By optimizing GPU clock frequencies dynamically during reinforcement learning post-training, this approach lowers electricity costs, reduces datacenter carbon footprints, and improves the sustainability of heavy AI training workloads without requiring tedious manual pre-tuning.

featured.title: Tug of Watts: A study on the Energy - Accuracy Trade-off of Large Language Models on Medical Question Answering Tasks
featured.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical question answering (QA) systems. While recent works aim at incrementally improving the downstream task accuracy, an empirical estimation of the models' energy consumption and the associated carbon footprints is often overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate how practitioners can estimate energy consumption and arrive at reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks available in the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard by investigating 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging from 270M to 14B parameters. We discuss how one can critically interpret energy versus accuracy trade-offs for a set of models for a given task. With this work, we underline that reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone does not suffice for careful trade-off assessments, but it also demands systematic construction and interpretation of joint trade-off metrics. We envisage such studies aiding practitioners in adopting better and more efficient models for their task and helping them become active participants in building sustainable LLM pipelines.

insight.tldr: The paper investigates the energy-accuracy trade-offs of deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) for medical question answering tasks, demonstrating how to evaluate models using joint metrics rather than disjoint ones.
insight.problem: While recent machine learning research focuses on incrementally improving downstream task accuracy in healthcare applications like medical question answering (QA), the associated energy consumption and carbon footprints during inference are frequently overlooked.
insight.approach: The authors examine 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging from 270M to 14B parameters on medical QA tasks from the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard. They use the CodeCarbon package to measure inference energy consumption and carbon emissions, and evaluate the models using joint trade-off metrics, Pareto-optimal frontiers, and a distance-based rating scheme.
key_findings: Investigated 13 LLMs from 3 model families ranging in size from 270M to 14B parameters.
Larger models achieve higher task performance but at the cost of significantly higher relative carbon footprints.
Reporting disjoint energy and accuracy metrics alone is insufficient for careful trade-off assessments; systematic joint metrics are required.
Utilized Pareto-optimal frontiers and a distance-based rating scheme to clearly distinguish the trade-offs of individual models.
insight.limitations: Not stated in the provided text.
insight.why_it_matters: It addresses the soaring energy demands of real-time AI inference (projected to reach 652 TWh by 2030) by providing practitioners with methods to jointly optimize energy consumption and accuracy, helping them choose more efficient models and build sustainable machine learning pipelines.

featured.title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
featured.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.

insight.tldr: The paper investigates the trade-offs between machine learning and lightweight link indicators for detecting wearer-induced non-line-of-sight (WNLOS) conditions in chest-worn UWB tags.
insight.problem: Wearer-induced non-line-of-sight (WNLOS) conditions cause significant UWB ranging errors, but existing detection methods often struggle to balance classification accuracy with the strict energy and runtime constraints of on-device processing.
insight.approach: The authors analyzed 21 classifiers—including machine learning (ML) models, radio link indicators (LI), and novel hybrid approaches—using a dataset of 1.5 million samples across various configurations.
key_findings: Relative performance of classifiers depends heavily on channel and PHY settings.
Some ML techniques provide only marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy than lightweight alternatives.
Hybrid classifiers effectively exploit the complementarity between ML and link indicators.
A recommender tool was introduced to help users identify optimal classifiers based on specific energy and accuracy constraints.
insight.limitations: Not stated in the provided text.
insight.why_it_matters: It addresses the sustainability of on-device intelligence by demonstrating that complex machine learning models are not always the most efficient choice, providing a tool to optimize energy consumption without sacrificing necessary performance.

more.title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
more.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

more.title: LanG 2.0: Energy-Efficient Agentic AI for Semi-Automated Security Operations at Scale
more.abstract: Security operations centers (SOCs) need to turn terabytes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted, affordable decisions to unveil hidden threats. We present LanG 2.0, an agentic system that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, investigating whether small local models can replace frontier models affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees. It incorporates entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Tests span eight flow datasets from five networks, real XDR alerts and multistage campaigns. Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81%, and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, scoring flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. The work demonstrates LanG's practical scalability, processing 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, over 30 million hourly, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering, so small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely.

more.title: HyVox: Rethinking Low-Power Voice Intelligence towards Neuromorphic-von Neumann Edge Computing
more.abstract: We present HyVox, a hybrid neuromorphic--von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification under tight energy budgets. HyVox splits the workload at the speaker embedding. A neuromorphic processor embeds the speech with sparse, event-driven computation, and a von Neumann microcontroller holds the speaker gallery and makes every decision: it scores queries by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype, with no weight update. On the neuromorphic processor, a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone learns a synaptic time constant per leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, allocating 832 neurons across fast, medium, and slow timescales. A 32-neuron spiking embedding extractor (SEE), pretrained on episodes that each enroll new speakers and reject outsiders, turns the backbone output into an embedding for speakers unseen in training; its 32 spike counts are the only interface between the two processors. To fit the chip's synapse and integer budgets, we compress the backbone 6.5x to 29.0k synapses, train it for integer bit-shift dynamics, and fine-tune it with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). CAST trains through a differentiable replica of the chip's integer neuron update, derived from its cycle-accurate simulator, so that gradient descent optimizes the exact weights and thresholds the chip runs; it doubles the top-1 accuracy of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. On 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 members and 94.9\% and 13.2\% with 20, and the network deployed on the neuromorphic chip matches its trained model. Each inference on a 3-s window takes 0.96 s and 1.63 mJ of dynamic energy, 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5x less dynamic and 5.8x less total energy than the most energy-efficient one.

more.title: BitLLM: Efficient Low-Bit, Conversion-Hiding LLM Decoding on Mobile GPUs
more.abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unlocked remarkable capabilities across various domains. However, deploying LLMs on mobile devices remains challenging because of their high computational and memory requirements. Low-bit quantization (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) can reduce model size while preserving accuracy, but its practical efficacy on mobile GPUs has been limited so far. In this paper, we identify that the performance gap stems primarily from frequent data type conversions between quantized and floating-point values, and dynamic and inefficient memory access patterns caused by the growing Key-Value (KV) cache during autoregressive decoding. We introduce BitLLM, a mobile inference engine that addresses type conversion overhead and suboptimal memory accesses in quantized LLMs. Our approach features an adaptive layout and packing strategy for the KV cache that ensures efficient memory access throughout LLM decoding. This is coupled with an integer-native execution pipeline that defers and overlaps type conversion outside the compute hot path, keeping the critical MatMul stages in the integer domain. Implemented on off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM outperforms leading engines, i.e., LLAMA.CPP, MNN-LLM, LiteRT-LM, and MLC-LLM, achieving average speedups of 1.78$\times$, 1.73$\times$, 1.58$\times$, and 1.47$\times$, respectively, across various models and quantization levels. Under long-context generation, BitLLM reduces average energy consumption (per token) by up to 88.9%.

more.title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
more.abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.

more.title: Superscalar Loop Processors
more.abstract: To sustain the computational demands of modern ML and HPC workloads, programmable accelerators integrate large arrays of processing elements (PEs), typically built around single-issue in-order cores to maximize integration density and energy efficiency. As a result, each PE's instruction throughput is upper-bounded at one instruction per cycle (IPC), often suffering from significant underutilization of its functional units (FUs). Conventional superscalar processors can improve FU utilization by increasing IPC, but they typically incur substantial area and energy overheads. This work proposes the Superscalar Loop Processor (SLP) architecture, a lightweight approach to superscalar execution that targets regular, compute-intensive loop kernels. We present the SLP execution model, which exploits the static structure of these workloads to enable efficient multiple-issue execution without the complexity of dynamic out-of-order scheduling. We demonstrate the SLP architecture through an open-source prototype implementation, Schnizo, developed as an enhancement of a tiny RV32I core with floating-point support. Across several ML and HPC microkernels, Schnizo achieves substantially higher IPC and FPU utilization than the scalar baseline while retaining the efficiency of lightweight in-order designs. These results demonstrate that SLPs can provide an efficient architectural solution for programmable accelerators targeting regular, compute-intensive workloads.

featured.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
featured.abstract: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

insight.tldr: FlowBatt is a conditional generative framework that uses flow matching and a diffusion transformer to predict probabilistic battery state-of-health (SOH) trajectories.
insight.problem: Existing machine learning methods for battery health primarily focus on deterministic point predictions for remaining useful life (RUL) or SOH, failing to capture the probabilistic nature of degradation trajectories across diverse chemistries.
insight.approach: The authors introduce FlowBatt, which uses a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to model full SOH degradation trajectories conditioned on early-cycle capacity data, while using explainable AI to optimize the input encoder.
key_findings: Achieved the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance across five public benchmark datasets.
Maintained prediction errors below 2.5% for SOH trajectories.
Delivered competitive RUL prediction performance compared to specialized baselines.
Provided empirical prediction intervals by generating multiple plausible degradation trajectories.
Reduced random forest RMSE and MAPE on the MATR-1 dataset by approximately 26% and 19% respectively using synthetic trajectories.
insight.limitations: The model lacks direct inputs for environmental factors like temperature or charging protocols, does not enforce physical constraints, and shows higher RUL errors and undercoverage of prediction intervals on specific datasets (MATR-2 and HUST).
insight.why_it_matters: It shifts battery management from simple point-based RUL estimation to probabilistic trajectory modeling, allowing for better uncertainty quantification and more robust health forecasting across heterogeneous battery chemistries.

featured.title: Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning for BESS Dispatch Under Renewable Uncertainty
featured.abstract: Battery energy storage system (BESS) flexibility depends on state of charge and intertemporal operating constraints. Renewable forecast errors of similar magnitudes can lead to different BESS dispatch results. An error may alter early charging or discharging decisions and reduce the flexibility available for subsequent regulation, while another may have little effect on the resulting schedule. To account for these unequal consequences, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL), which trains renewable predictors using the realized operating costs of their induced BESS schedules. Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation provide training feedback without requiring differentiating through the non-differentiable mixed-integer BESS dispatch problem. The same decision feedback is further combined with prediction sensitivity to develop a decision-oriented XAI method that identifies the input features and forecast periods most consequential to BESS operation. Case studies using German wind and solar data show that FC-DFL reduces the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% relative to accuracy-based predict-then-optimize method. The XAI analysis further demonstrates that the identified high-impact forecast periods produce 2.84 times larger average absolute changes in realized operating cost than low-impact periods. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating downstream decision-making outcomes into renewable forecasting and demonstrate the value of FC-DFL in improving BESS regulation and providing operationally meaningful forecast explanations.

featured.title: Cross-Domain Joint-Embedding Pretraining For Heterogeneous Industrial Time Series
featured.abstract: Industrial predictive maintenance and manufacturing tasks frequently contain abundant sensor measurements, but with limited labeled data. We investigate cross-domain self-supervised pretraining using joint-embedding predictive architecture for heterogeneous industrial time series (JEPA-HITS), which learns one encoder from various domains such as battery, semiconductor chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), computer numerical control (CNC) machining, and bearing while preserving dataset-specific temporal scales. We evaluate representation reuse on regression and classification problems under reduced-label downstream training, and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) pretraining. Compared with the same architecture initialized randomly, LODO pretraining reduces RMSE from 10.72 to 7.95 on battery remaining useful life (RUL), 4.34 to 3.89 on CMP, and 13.53 to 11.72 on tool wear regression, while improving bearing fault diagnosis macro-F1 from 0.547 to 0.737. Overall results suggest that unlabeled time series measurements from heterogeneous industrial processes can provide reusable representations for downstream learning with limited labeled data.
